deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page treats plane geometry with complex numbers, and the next page treats a spherical-triangle locus. This page sets up the Mercator projection of the unit sphere ('Halbmesser immer = 1') in complex form, and transfers the half-angle analogies of a spherical triangle into Mercator coordinates.

Notation (Gauss's): x = abscissa = longitude; y = ordinate = Mercator latitude; u = geographic latitude belonging to y; s = great-circle distance between (x,y) and (x',y'); theta, theta' = angles that the arc s (its tangents at the two endpoints) makes with the abscissa line, i.e. with the parallel/east direction.

(1) Mercator ordinate. y = log tan(45deg + u/2). In modern terms y = gd^{-1}(u) and u = gd(y), the Gudermannian. Gauss writes the hyperbolic functions as circular functions of imaginary argument:
- tan(iy/2) = i tan(u/2), i.e. tanh(y/2) = tan(u/2).
- sin(iy) = i tan u, i.e. sinh y = tan u.
- tan(iy) = i sin u, i.e. tanh y = sin u.
- cos(iy) = 1/cos u, i.e. cosh y = sec u.
- cos(iy/2) = cos(u/2)/sqrt(cos u) = cos(u/2) sqrt(cos iy).
He labels cos iy = sec u the 'Vergrösserungsverhältniss', the linear scale (magnification) factor of the Mercator map.

(2) Transfer of the spherical-triangle analogies. Take the triangle formed by the pole N and the two points P=(x,y), P'=(x',y') (my reconstruction of the set-up):
- angle at N: C = x'-x;
- side a = 90deg - u' (opposite P), side b = 90deg - u (opposite P'), side c = s;
- angle at P: A = 90deg - theta; angle at P': B = 90deg + theta'.
The Gauss (Delambre/Mollweide) analogies are:
- cos(c/2) sin((A+B)/2) = cos(C/2) cos((a-b)/2)
- cos(c/2) cos((A+B)/2) = sin(C/2) cos((a+b)/2)
- sin(c/2) sin((A-B)/2) = cos(C/2) sin((a-b)/2)
- sin(c/2) cos((A-B)/2) = sin(C/2) sin((a+b)/2)

The step needed to rewrite them (my filling-in): from tan(u/2) = tanh(y/2) we get cos(u/2) = sqrt(cos u) cosh(y/2) and sin(u/2) = sqrt(cos u) sinh(y/2). Writing h = sqrt(cosh y cosh y') = 1/sqrt(cos u cos u'), this gives:
- cos((u'-u)/2) = cosh((y'+y)/2)/h
- cos((u'+u)/2) = cosh((y'-y)/2)/h
- sin((u'-u)/2) = sinh((y'-y)/2)/h
- sin((u'+u)/2) = sinh((y'+y)/2)/h

Substituting yields exactly Gauss's four equations:
- cos(dx/2) sin(i dy/2) = i sin((theta+theta')/2) sin(s/2) h
- sin(dx/2) cos(i dy/2) = cos((theta+theta')/2) sin(s/2) h
- cos(dx/2) cos(i(y+y')/2) = cos((theta-theta')/2) cos(s/2) h
- sin(dx/2) sin(i(y+y')/2) = i sin((theta-theta')/2) cos(s/2) h
Here dx = x'-x, dy = y'-y, and h = sqrt(cos iy cos iy').

(3) Complex combination. Put t = x+iy and t' = x'+iy'. Adding the second equation to the first gives
sin((t'-t)/2) = h sin(s/2) [cos((theta+theta')/2) + i sin((theta+theta')/2)] = h sin(s/2) e^{(i/2)(theta+theta')}.
In words: modulus |sin((t'-t)/2)| = h sin(s/2), which is an exact chord-length formula in Mercator coordinates. Argument = half the sum of the two endpoint bearings. A started formula for the sum t+t' is struck out.

(4) Tangent forms, obtained by dividing the equations (cross-referenced to the 'grünes Buch'):
- first by second: i tan((theta+theta')/2) = tan(i dy/2)/tan(dx/2);
- fourth by third: i tan((theta-theta')/2) = tan(dx/2) tan(i(y+y')/2).
These give the half-sum and half-difference of the endpoint bearings directly from the Mercator coordinates.

(5) Approximation for short distances ('Hinreichend genau ist immer'): (1 + (1/48)(dx^2 - dy^2)) sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) = h sin(s/2). This is a small-argument expansion of |sin((t'-t)/2)|. My expansion gives instead: |sin(w/2)| ~ (|w|/2)(1 - Re(w^2)/24), with w = t'-t.
errors: Sign of the exponent: Gauss's own four equations give sin((t'-t)/2) = h e^{+i(theta+theta')/2} sin(s/2). The page appears to show e^{-i(theta+theta')/2}. Either this is a slip, a different orientation convention for theta, or a misreading of the exponent.

The final approximation does not match the exact relation as written. Expanding |sin(w/2)| for w = (x'-x) + i(y'-y) gives (1/2) sqrt(dx^2+dy^2) (1 - (dx^2-dy^2)/24) = h sin(s/2). The page as transcribed has no factor 1/2 (unless the RHS actually reads 2h sin(s/2)), and its correction term is +1/48 instead of -1/24. Equivalently, the correct form is sqrt(dx^2+dy^2)(1 - (dx^2-dy^2)/24) = 2h sin(s/2). Possibly Gauss intended a different arrangement, but as transcribed it is inconsistent with the exact formula above it.
Minor: the struck-out fragments ('cos 1/2', 'sin 1/2(t+t) =') are abandoned attempts, presumably at a companion formula for the sum t+t'.

results.what: Mercator ordinate y = log tan(45deg+u/2), with the identities tanh(y/2)=tan(u/2), sinh y=tan u, tanh y=sin u, cosh y=sec u (scale factor), written as circular functions of imaginary argument
results.modern_name: Gudermannian function / inverse Gudermannian; Mercator scale factor sec(phi)
results.usually_credited_to: Mercator/Wright (projection); Lambert (1760s-70s, hyperbolic functions); Gudermann (1830s, the function's name)

results.what: The four Gauss/Delambre analogies for the pole-point-point triangle, rewritten in Mercator coordinates (longitude difference, Mercator latitudes, endpoint bearings, distance)
results.modern_name: Delambre (Gauss, Mollweide) analogies applied to the Mercator/rhumb geometry

results.what: Complex form sin((t'-t)/2) = h e^{i(theta+theta')/2} sin(s/2), with t = x+iy and h = sqrt(cosh y cosh y'): exact chord formula plus the half-sum of bearings as the argument
results.modern_name: Chordal (spherical) metric pulled back to Mercator coordinates: chord = 2|sin(dt/2)|/sqrt(cosh y cosh y'); equivalently the stereographic chordal metric via z = e^{it}
results.usually_credited_to: chordal metric on the Riemann sphere: 19th c. (Riemann/Neumann era); complex treatment of conformal maps: Lagrange 1779, Gauss 1822/25

results.what: Tangent formulas: i tan((theta+theta')/2) = tan(i dy/2)/tan(dx/2) and i tan((theta-theta')/2) = tan(dx/2) tan(i(y+y')/2)
results.modern_name: Napier's analogies in Mercator variables (geodesic bearings from Mercator coordinates)

results.what: Short-distance approximation of the great-circle distance from Mercator coordinates
results.modern_name: Series correction for great-circle distance on a conformal map (scale-factor correction)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's geodetic projection work (Hannover survey, 1820s); Krüger later

deep.surprise_reason: The ingredients are known: Gauss's analogies, the Mercator projection, and Gauss's well-known use of complex variables for conformal maps. Packaging the spherical-triangle analogies into one complex identity in t = x+iy is elegant. It amounts to the chordal metric on the sphere written in Mercator coordinates, with the bearings appearing as the argument. If this dates to around 1809 it is a nice early instance of Gauss's complex-variable approach to conformal projections. It is not a major result credited to someone else.

checkable.asserts: tan(iy/2) = i tan(u/2), i.e. tanh(y/2) = tan(u/2) (Gudermannian)
sinh y = tan u, tanh y = sin u, cosh y = sec u (all evaluate to 0)
cos(iy/2) = cos(u/2)/sqrt(cos u) = cos(u/2) sqrt(cos iy) (both 0)

checkable.sympy: u,u2,dx=0.5,0.9,0.4; y=sp.log(sp.tan(sp.pi/4+u/2)); y2=sp.log(sp.tan(sp.pi/4+u2/2)); s=sp.acos(sp.sin(u)*sp.sin(u2)+sp.cos(u)*sp.cos(u2)*sp.cos(dx)); h=sp.sqrt(sp.cosh(y)*sp.cosh(y2)); sp.N(sp.Abs(sp.sin((dx+sp.I*(y2-y))/2)) - h*sp.sin(s/2))
checkable.asserts: |sin((t'-t)/2)| = h sin(s/2) exactly (gives 0): the chordal-distance formula in Mercator coordinates

checkable.sympy: u,u2,dx=0.5,0.9,0.4; y=sp.log(sp.tan(sp.pi/4+u/2)); y2=sp.log(sp.tan(sp.pi/4+u2/2)); A=sp.atan2(sp.sin(dx)*sp.cos(u2), sp.cos(u)*sp.sin(u2)-sp.sin(u)*sp.cos(u2)*sp.cos(dx)); B=sp.atan2(sp.sin(dx)*sp.cos(u), -(sp.cos(u2)*sp.sin(u)-sp.sin(u2)*sp.cos(u)*sp.cos(dx))); th=sp.pi/2-A; th2=B-sp.pi/2; sp.N(sp.I*sp.tan((th+th2)/2) - sp.tan(sp.I*(y2-y)/2)/sp.tan(dx/2))
checkable.asserts: i tan((theta+theta')/2) = tan(i(y'-y)/2)/tan((x'-x)/2), with theta = 90deg - azimuth at P and theta' = (angle at P') - 90deg (should be 0)
sin(w/2) = w/2 - w^3/48 + ..., so |sin(w/2)| ~ (|w|/2)(1 - Re(w^2)/24); Re(w^2) = dx^2 - dy^2. This checks the coefficient in the final approximate formula.

transcription_corrections: The exponent in 'sin 1/2(t'-t) = h e^{-1/2 i(theta+theta')} sin 1/2 s' should be checked against the image. The page's own four equations imply the exponent +1/2 i(theta+theta').
In the final line the RHS 'h sin 1/2 s' should be checked; it may read '2h sin 1/2 s', since consistency with the exact formula requires a factor 2 (or 1/2 on the left).

The struck-out 'sqrt(cos iy . cos iy') = h' on the t-line was rewritten to the right of the next line. The struck '[cos 1/2]' after sin 1/2 s and the struck 'sin 1/2(t+t) =' (probably t'+t) are abandoned fragments.
The dotted bracket labelled 'Vergrösserungsverhältniss' points to cos iy = 1/cos u (the scale factor), not to the whole block.
The pencil marks 'Z21X X.17'-like and 'Hv' are later archival/library annotations, not Gauss's text.
